item.title: Advancing Technology Is the New Existential Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

Advancing Technology Is the New Existential Anxiety

Much like midcentury concerns about nuclear war, technology is today's anxiety.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Emerging technology may be this era's existential crisis, as many people feel a loss of autonomy.
  • Much like the anxiety of the Cold War era, the AI era has produced a societal sense of worry.
  • Counterbalancing worry with optimism can help navigate the uncertainties of advancing technology.

In a May 2026 survey conducted by the American Psychological Association, more than half of the participants identified “the impact of emerging technology in everyday life” as an issue they were somewhat or very anxious about (APA, 2026). The seemingly unstoppable emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) seems to be driving this rise in tech-related anxiety, so much so that recently a new psychological concept, “AI Anxiety,” has begun to appear in scholarly articles and research. Advancing technology, which was once viewed as a mainly positive development that could improve our lives, is beginning to be seen more as an existential threat that could lead to our downfall. According to the Pew Research Center, concern about AI now heavily outweighs excitement, with a jump from 31% of respondents feeling concerned to 55% since 2021 (McClain & Park, 2026).

Evolving Societal Concerns

Over time, societal concerns evolve and change, and our collective psychology evolves along with these broader changes. For example, in psychology texts from the midcentury, worries about the Cold War, nuclear annihilation, and the atomic bomb were often referenced as the main anxieties of the period. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), “the political and military tension between the U.S. and the Soviet Union fostered a profound anxiety in our nation during the 1950s,” driven by “the atomic explosions at Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945…[and] the horrors of nuclear warfare” (Moore & Moore, 2009). While there remains an underlying societal anxiety about war and nuclear capability, these fears seem much less tangible than they perhaps did in the 1950s and have been replaced by fears related to loss of autonomy due to rapidly advancing technology.

The Loss of Autonomy

In a 2024 article, Johannessen et al. point out that people typically want to control their own decision-making process; however, rapidly advancing technology and AI often cause us to feel that we are losing our ability to control this process and that our free will and autonomy are being directly threatened. In response to this, the European Commission passed into law an Artificial Intelligence Act that requires medical AI to have “explainability,” which can be enhanced with “causability” to promote better understanding of the rationale underlying AI decisions (Plass et al., 2023). In other words, the European Union now requires that AI have a greater level of transparency, particularly for high-risk AI systems, such as those that are used in healthcare. In the United States, however, no such sweeping guideline or law has been passed, and AI continues to evolve and grow without specific regulations. An article in the Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology describes AI as having its own autonomy, “which means AI is out of human control, thus there is concern that AI may autonomously harm human beings” (Johnson & Verdicchio, 2017). This threat to personal autonomy and decision-making can cause significant anxiety.

The Existential Threat

We might view the current realities about emerging and advancing technology as this era’s existential threat, much like the nuclear annihilation worries of the midcentury. According to the APA, existential anxiety is characterized by “angst associated with one’s freedom as a human being to make choices” (APA, 2026). In my private practice, I currently work with multiple clients in the tech industry who feel concerned that AI will eliminate their jobs and that there is not much they can do to prevent it. This is not necessarily an irrational fear that has no basis, much as fears of nuclear war in the 1950s were not necessarily irrational either. When existential worry becomes rampant, feelings of hopelessness and helplessness can result, yet another blow to our sense of personal autonomy.

Counterbalancing Worry

In the 1950s, despite the looming possibilities of negative outcomes related to nuclear capability, people did continue to live their lives—they had families, worked, went about their daily business, and engaged in their lives. Midcentury psychologist and author Rollo May wrote of the strange duality of a sky that at once could be expansive and beautiful but was also the place from which an atomic bomb could fall. In a sense, we are living in a similar reality: the advancement of technology has produced countless benefits, yet it comes with great risk at the same time. May’s point was that it was worth seeing the sky as beautiful every now and then rather than as a constant, impending threat.

In practical terms, this counterbalancing of two distinct realities might take the form of engaging less with technology, connecting more with your present life, relationships, and self-care, and recognizing that there will always be a societal threat, no matter the era. From there, we can find a collective will to cope rather than to give in to existential fears. Sanae Okamoto, a psychologist and behavioral scientist at the United Nations University–Maastricht Economic and Social Research Institute on Innovation and Technology in the Netherlands, reminds us that “we’re all in this challenge together” and that confronting AI anxiety begins with “building solidarity, finding community and coming up with collective solutions” (Leffer, 2023). Indeed, finding ways to counterbalance our worry with collectiveness and solidarity can help us navigate a time in history that will undoubtedly be written about in many psychological texts, just as the Cold War era was.

item.title: How to Help Boys Build a Moral Purpose
item.description:
Parenting

How to Help Boys Build a Moral Purpose

Small experiences can help boys discover that it feels good to do good.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • When boys feel that they matter, they can begin to discover the value of doing good for others.
  • Don’t just tell boys they matter. Let them experience mattering.
  • Responsibility for the common good creates a moral purpose which is motivating.
Source: Vitor Luciano/Pexels

Rules, boundaries, setbacks and difficulties should not be removed from our boys' lives. These challenges create the optimal conditions to learn, adapt and build the skills to grow. When a boy struggles and eventually finds a way through, he learns more than the skill itself. He learns a different story: Maybe I can do difficult things. And even more powerfully, Maybe I have worth and something to offer my world.

Challenge is essential for growth.

Boys still absorb powerful negative messages about masculinity: Cope on your own, don’t be vulnerable and don’t ask for help. These work against trying and failing, or even attempting. For modern parents and teachers, rather than removing difficulties, we must help our boy find ways to ask for help and find the resources he needs. And rather than simply saying, You need to ask for help when you get stuck, or Work through it, you can offer a greater motivation—a higher purpose, greater than the problem or the person, something for someone else.

This is the power of moral purpose.

When I was younger, a boy in my class was unbelievably badly behaved. All of the things he did—undermining the teacher, being dishonest with his parents, starting fights—were acts of anger.

At best he was disengaged. At worst he was a nightmare.

But then a strange thing happened. He went on a notoriously hard school camp, with early morning ice swims, running, and strict rules. For some kids, this wouldn’t work, but it was exactly what this boy needed. He won the prize for best at camp. All of his previous experiences of hardship made for the perfect preparation for this new environment. Best of all, the camp leaders trusted him to lead other students. They gave him the moral purpose to care for others.

And in that moment, he learned to care for himself.

What do we want to make possible for our boys?

As parents, teachers and coaches, we spend a lot of time thinking about behaviours we want to stop in boys. But we should be asking a different question: What are the behaviours we want to start?

Telling boys to be good and pointing to good role models might help, but nothing is better than experiencing a positive cycle in which good behaviour is not only valued but needed for success. This is where moral purpose begins: Our boys can learn that doing good things helps them to feel good, and to belong.

The virtuous cycle of mattering

There is an important distinction between telling a boy that he matters and creating experiences through which he discovers that he matters. Imagine a boy arrives somewhere and an adult greets him with: "Good to see you, I need help with something—and I think you might be just the right person to help me."

Immediately, he feels needed, and his purpose has a positive direction.

Developmental psychologist Lawrence Kohlberg argued that children’s moral reasoning develops over time, from a focus on self-interest (and avoiding punishment) towards greater concerns for relationships.

It also points to the fact that for us to have good relationships, we need to do good things. You can’t separate the two. This is where the cycle begins.

Source: Amet Zeki/Pexels

The steps to help build moral purpose

Listen. Give our boys structures through which they can talk aloud and think through their choices. Using our voice is how our earliest thoughts are formed and how our actions are determined. Using structures to promote discussion, listening to boys and inviting comment is the first stage. (Click here to read about my WIN model.)

Improve their media diet. We must intentionally introduce good stories and role models. One of the best ways for us to think about morality is to think not simply in terms of right and wrong, but in terms of the common good. Stories often have a built-in moral or ethical position that can become part of a discussion. For younger boys, read Aesop’s fables, or the stories of Hans Christian Anderson. As they get older, rather than simply giving them good stories, help them unpack the stories they are witness to.

Give them real problems to solve. Challenge them! Put the boys in your life to work for social change. Give them a job, something with responsibility. But to do this, give them the problem, not the solution. It may seem the wrong way around but ask them to solve something for the common good. Here is an example:

I was thinking about that girl in your class that you were telling me about. You know, you were saying how she always seemed alone. What’s one thing you could do to help her tomorrow?

Or, if their room is often untidy, rather than simply saying to your son, Keep it tidy or there will be consequences, try:

I'm stuck on this problem. We’ve talked a lot about the house and when I get back from work there is often mess. How can we fix this? [Discuss]. What will be the consequences if we don’t stick to this, do you think? [Let him determine that too.]

Notice when he does the right thing. It doesn’t need to be a big deal, nor does the outcome need to be the only thing that’s noticed. Notice what his work is doing and talk to that. Engage that part in a conversation.

If we want our boys to do good things of consequence, we need to let them know that what they do matters. We must give them opportunities to discover it for themselves. If we want them to persist when they feel like it's too hard to ask for help, we need to give them a higher cause.

item.title: 6 Questions to Help You Design Your Life
item.description:
Happiness

6 Questions to Help You Design Your Life

You don’t have to just react to what life throws your way.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • We can choose to react to our life or create it by proactively mapping out our goals and priorities.
  • The keys are defining what gives you purpose, your values, and imagining your ideal everyday life.
  • The challenges are avoding these questions by being passive, distracting yourself, or accepting what you get,
Source: Fredy_Marinez_Photograph / Pixabay

You’ve undoubtedly heard the phrase, “Life is what you make it.” At first glance, it seems to be about responding to and accommodating the challenges and opportunities, problems and hardships that come with being alive. But you can also hear it as a call to be proactive—the making—where life is less a workaround and more like a lump of clay you can shape and mold as you see fit.

Here are six questions and their challenges to help you design your life:

1. What do you want to invest your life doing?

This is the question you likely struggled with in high school or at the start of college—essentially, what do you want to be when you grow up?

The challenge is to think outside the box—not be constrained by family or cultural expectations—and tap into your potential: your talents and skills, passion, and sense of purpose.

2. What do you want your everyday life to be like?

If the first question is about the big picture, this is about life in the details, the day-to-day behaviors that make a good day: time with family and friends, balancing time for self and time for others, and setting priorities.

The challenge is that you don’t set priorities and instead fall victim to your own routines and lifestyle. You become reactive and passive rather than proactive and creative. Rather than running your life, your life runs you.

3. What does it mean to be an adult?

This is about values; you choose what a responsible adult and a good person look like. Again, it is about setting priorities, regulating your emotions, and ultimately crafting your self-image.

The challenges, driven by passivity, are two: Rather than defining your values, you substitute rules and blindly adhere to the shoulds handed down by parents and people in authority. The other is that you believe you’re powerless to change your personality—“That’s just the way I am” becomes your motto, an excuse to avoid the work of shaping yourself. Just as you can become a victim of your lifestyle, you can also become a victim of yourself.

4. How do you want to treat others?

If the question above is about shaping you, this is about shaping relationships—with partners, children, colleagues, and strangers. Again, imagine, set standards, and take action.

The challenge is that you forget you get back what you put out and that the world will gladly adapt to whatever lens you choose to look through. If you mistreat others, they will likely mistreat you. If you see others as manipulative, dangerous, or competitive, you will certainly find them, but you’ll undoubtedly be anxious and lonely.

5. What is the ultimate purpose of it all?

What is the meaning of life? Do you believe, like the Stoics, that life is an opportunity to be virtuous in the face of adversity? Do you think, like Buddha, that it is about attaining enlightenment, or, like Nietzsche, that it is about being creative and living up to your potential? Or, like the existentialists, that life is about building a life through choices and personal responsibility? Or, like Jesus, that it is about love and serving others, or, like Epicurus or Whitman, that life is about simply experiencing and savoring it?

The challenge is that you avoid the question by staying busy, accepting others’ answers, or failing to translate your beliefs into concrete action.

6. What do you want the moral of your life to be?

What would you like others to say about you at your funeral? What epitaph would you want on your tombstone? How do you need to live to have the fewest regrets?

Leave room for change

Your answers to some of these questions may change over time as you grow older and hopefully wiser, as life experiences do their own shaping. Keep your ear close to the ground so your life stays in lockstep with you, and so your outer life reflects your inner one.

And maybe that’s the biggest challenge of all.

item.title: The Benefits of Multi-Generational Family Support
item.description:
Parenting

The Benefits of Multi-Generational Family Support

Grandparents can be a significant source of support. It's a win, win, win.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Grandparent involvement offers myriad multigenerational benefits.
  • The benefits of close relationships between children and grandparents extend well into adulthood.
  • Seniors benefit both socially and cognitively.

Multigenerational households are a growing trend in the US and Canada. Many sources cite economic reasons—the lack of affordable housing, childcare, and senior housing—but the benefits extend well beyond the financial. For many supporters of multi-generational family engagement, this trend is welcome news. In his recently published book, The Art and Science of Parenting and Grandparenting: Raising Emotionally Healthy Children in a Challenging World, author Kenneth Barish, Ph.D., clinical professor of psychology at Weill Cornell Medicine and a fellow of the American Psychological Association, explored the multigenerational benefits of grandparent involvement. He found that we all need close others who listen, especially children. This may ease their loneliness, show that conflict is not the end of the world, and that life challenges are surmountable.

Recent research findings offer an impressive list of benefits of close, multigenerational ties and active grandparent involvement in daily family life for all three generations.

For grandparents
For grandparents, involvement in their grandchildren’s lives yields significant cognitive benefits and positively affects their social well-being. According to research published by the American Psychological Association in January of 2026 involving close to three thousand grandparents who participated in a longitudinal study of aging examining the impact of their participation in their grandchildren’s childcare and leisure activities, those who were actively involved in the lives of their grandchildren “scored higher on tests of both memory and verbal fluency compared with those who didn’t.”

The Harvard Study of Adult Development, the world’s longest-running study on well-being, recognized the central role of deep relationships in long-term health, life satisfaction, and happiness, and credits assisting grandchildren with homework, babysitting, and playing with them with possibly staving off cognitive decline.

Additional research that examined the benefits of caregiving by activity, type, and frequency also linked caregiving to increased episodic memory and verbal fluency in seniors, and found that grandparents who regularly picked up their grandchildren from school or daycare, and were available to step in and provide childcare when required, exhibited higher verbal fluency than grandparents who provided these supports on a less frequent basis.

Furthermore, an intergenerational pilot study exploring the benefits of engagement between children and seniors reported decreased negative stereotyping of seniors and improved well-being among seniors after participating in a weekly intergenerational summer camp.

For parents, the sandwich generation
According to recent statistics, more than half of adults in their 40s are members of the sandwich generation. A recent study determined that this generation struggles with several significant challenges, including: “time management issues, physical exhaustion, stress, and caregiver burnout.” The study concluded that parents and in-laws are a significant source of support.

For grandchildren
The myriad short- and long-term benefits of grandparent involvement in the lives of children and young adults are profound. A 2025 study on multigenerational families in contemporary China, where grandparents share childcare responsibilities, determined that: “Grandparents’ involvement may help to relieve perceived mothers’ parenting stress and enhance family strengths, thereby indirectly affecting young children’s resilience.”

The positive effect of grandparent involvement continues long after childhood. A 2025 survey of emerging and young adults (age 18 to 29) found that social support from one or more grandparents contributed to their current emotional well-being, regardless of whether that grandparent was still alive, even among individuals who had experienced poor care from their parents or primary caregivers. Bareish sees such involvement as a win, win, win.

Six steps to build and maintain strong intergenerational connections
Be proactive: Besides the usual holiday and birthday celebrations, create opportunities for informal family gatherings. In regular, informal get-togethers, everyone is likely to feel more relaxed.
Encourage one-on-one time. One-on-one time helps grandparents and grandchildren build strong personal relationships and genuinely connect. If family members live far away, encourage everyone to keep in touch and use online platforms that allow for face-to-face communication.
Set an example for your children by spending time with your family members and including your parents and their friends in your life.
Accept that conflicts will likely arise, and try to address situations with compassion and patience.
Maintain healthy and positive communication. Keep the lines of communication open: Don’t let small misunderstandings fester into long-term resentment. By communicating clearly and compassionately, you can reduce misunderstandings and resentment.
Seek the help of a family therapist if your family is struggling with conflict or life challenges like illness, transitioning into long-term care, or other significant and distressing changes.

item.title: How I Lost My Temper Over a Broken Bottle
item.description:
Parenting

How I Lost My Temper Over a Broken Bottle

Personal Perspective: Modeling how to argue and fight at home is the piece we're missing.

Posted September 23, 2026

Anger
Source: Dogan Alpaslan Demir from Pixabay

At the store, I gave my son a bag and told him to be careful; it contained a glass bottle. I told him to hold it firmly. But he did not. The bag fell and hit the floor, and the bottle broke.

I loudly overreacted just outside the store. At the time, as I was yelling, I knew my reaction didn't match the size of the bottle; I had overreacted, as many of us do, and I had no control over it.

In the car, he started in and did not stop: How I overreacted. How it was only a bottle. How I always overreact. And I sat there driving, getting smaller, shrinking, carrying out the analyzing in a way that every parent goes through, the one which ends in being a terrible mother.

Then about halfway home, I realized: I am allowed to be angry!

I am allowed to be upset in a supermarket about a broken bottle. It was not a great reaction. But it was human, and it cannot break us; if it can, then something is terribly wrong. This movement seems small, but it was transformative in the way I related to my anger and reactions as a parent.

The Half of the Curriculum We Skip

Most of the time, parents focus on kindness: sharing, using words, and saying sorry. The other half of what we were taught was harder: How to be furious at someone you love and still be at the table with them that night. How to say the sharp thing, the one you would take back, and then find your way back from it.
We raise children who can collaborate and cannot argue. As soon as they detect tension, they go silent, or they erupt and then subside, since we never showed them what comes next.

Attunement, Misattunement, and Reattunement

People often refer to attunement as if it were harmony, but it isn't; it is about tracking, which means engaging nonverbally with another person in a manner that gives them full and responsive attention. You pick up on his rhythm, his breath, and get close enough that he feels understood. It has much more to do with accuracy than with being nice. Misattunement means a mistake: either you stop keeping track, or you track incorrectly. We all misattune; it is a part of ordinary, routine life. Reattunement refers to the action you take in response.

With Expressive Trauma Integration, the aim is not to achieve attunement and then stay there, but to move continuously between all three states.

Ed Tronick, after years of filming parents and infants frame by frame, discovered that ordinary, well-functioning pairs—all of them—are out of sync about 70 percent of the time. What mattered in all that footage was what happened next.

It creates a sense of responsibility, and for parents who are making an effort, it comes quickly. However, observe what it teaches: If every time I get angry I collapse, then my son will conclude that anger is catastrophic and that the person who gets angry must be destroyed.

There is a real difference between I am allowed to have this reaction and my reaction has no cost. But you repay that responsibility by coming back, not by shrinking. A parent flat on the floor with guilt is unavailable, which is exactly what their child does not need.

Reattunement and Concern for the Other

Almost no one is taught how to reattune, and most of what people call reattuning is actually something different. An apology is mainly about me and my feelings afterward, while reattunement is about being concerned with the other, in this case a child. "Sorry, buddy” isn't enough, nor is asking the child to say it's okay too, since that would place the responsibility for reconciling the situation on him.

Start by calming down because it's impossible to readjust while within the flood. Then name it, without a defense clause and without any "but": "I overreacted in the store. That was a lot, and it was about more than the bottle. Sometimes I overreact. That is not an excuse; it is me telling you I know it was too much. I am sorry." And do not retract the anger itself. Reattunement does not mean pretending you weren't angry. It means both things stand: I was angry, I overreacted, and I am still here.

Then let your child have their response, no matter how long their rant is. My son's rant was him doing what I want him to be able to do at 30 with a boss or a partner. He told the person who had just alarmed him that she had alarmed him, out loud, at length, to her face, and he did it without leaving. I want him to keep that. A child who goes quiet instead is telling you something else.

I told him this at home: The overreaction, the aspect which had nothing to do with the bottle, and the fact that no sentence was used to take the anger back. He accepted it and returned to what he was doing.

You move on only when the room once again seems ordinary, not when somebody has offered a sufficient apology.

What the Body Learns

Each cycle of miss and return teaches something words do not. Someone gets loud, and someone comes back. Over hundreds of repetitions, it becomes something his body expects, long after he has forgotten the bottle. He learns to survive anger without feeling destroyed by it.

That is what he learned—not about having a childhood without conflict, which nobody gets.

So now I say it out loud, when things have cooled: You are allowed to be angry at me. I am allowed to be angry at you. Neither of us is going anywhere. We can survive this.

Note: With a younger child, you could say: I am angry with you, and I love you. I can be upset and love at the same time.

item.title: The Other Side of Medical Gaslighting
item.description:
Gaslighting

The Other Side of Medical Gaslighting

Most conversations focus on patients. A new paper asks what happens to doctors.

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • Epistemic injustice in medicine has two sides: patient deficit and doctor excess.
  • Doctors’ epistemic privilege actively reshapes how they perceive patients.
  • Most medical dismissal is not based on bad intentions, but structural imbalance.
Source: Sasun Bughdaryan / Unsplash

Most accounts of medical gaslighting follow the same arc: A patient presents with symptoms, they are dismissed, told it is stress, told the tests are normal, told to come back if things get worse. They leave without answers, sometimes wondering whether they imagined the whole thing. Eventually, perhaps years later, a diagnosis arrives that confirms what they had been saying all along.

That experience is well documented. Women, people of colour, and patients with conditions that lack clear biomarkers can face difficulties being believed, and the consequences of being dismissed can be serious.

But there is another person in the story who rarely gets examined: the doctor who did the dismissing.

A paper published this month in Philosophical Psychology argues that this is an important omission. Lucienne Spencer suggests that when we talk about epistemic injustice in medicine, we tend to focus on the person whose experience and knowledge is being discounted. We pay much less attention to what happens to the person whose knowledge is routinely given more weight (Spencer, 2026).

How Doctors Exercise Epistemic Privilege

Spencer describes this unequal distribution of credibility as epistemic privilege. Doctors enter clinical encounters with an authority that patients do not have. They have the training, the institutional position, the medical vocabulary and, often, access to tests and clinical information that the patient cannot interpret on their own.

Obviously, medicine needs expertise and doctors have trained for decades. The problem is what happens when that authority becomes so familiar it starts to feel unquestionable.

Drawing on Merleau-Ponty’s philosophy of embodiment, Spencer makes a more unusual argument: Epistemic privilege is not simply something a doctor has. Over time, it can become part of how they experience and interpret the clinical encounter. In other words, it may influence both what a doctor thinks and what they notice in the first place. A clinician who has spent years being treated as the person with the answers may become accustomed to occupying that position. A patient’s interpretation of their own symptoms can then arrive as information that has already been unconsciously assigned a different weight.

That is a much harder problem to solve than telling doctors to be less biased.

The Other Side of Medical Dismissal

This changes the way we think about medical dismissal.

If epistemic privilege can influence perception itself, then the problem is not simply that some doctors behave badly or hold conscious biases. The clinical environment may also shape what feels credible, what seems relevant and what gets noticed. Much of the advice given to patients assumes that the problem is primarily on their side of the interaction: They should keep a symptom diary and bring notes. They should ask questions, and if they don't agree they should get a second opinion. And they should learn the medical terminology and be persistent.

All of those things can help, but this is still asking the person with less institutional authority to work harder to overcome the imbalance.

Spencer’s argument looks at the other side of the equation. If patients can spend years learning that they have to fight to be believed, clinicians can spend years in an environment in which their interpretation is rarely required to fight for credibility.

I Am Writing This as a Patient, Too

I work in neuropathology, so I know what it is like to occupy the other side of that imbalance. I understand what it means for a clinician’s interpretation of evidence to carry institutional weight.

I also know what it feels like to be the patient.

When your own symptoms require letters, appointments and precise clinical language just to be taken seriously, you become very aware of how much easier it is to be heard when you already speak the language of medicine.

That has made Spencer’s argument particularly interesting to me. The issue may not always be that a doctor consciously decides not to believe a patient. Sometimes the problem may begin earlier, with what the clinician has learned to recognise as important evidence.

This is uncomfortable because it does not require anyone to be malicious. Most medical dismissal is not an elaborate act of cruelty: Doctors are working within systems that reward certain forms of evidence, rely heavily on clinical experience and place enormous responsibility on their judgement. They are also human beings whose expectations are shaped by years of practice.

Structural Change in Clinical Environments

If epistemic privilege can become embedded in how clinicians perceive their patients, then improving the situation requires more than teaching doctors to be better listeners; it requires structural change.

We need clinical environments in which patient testimony is not automatically treated as something to be confirmed or overruled by medical evidence, but as evidence in its own right. A patient may not know what is causing their symptoms. They may misunderstand what a test means. They may even be wrong about what is happening. None of that makes their experience irrelevant.

The point is not to replace medical expertise with patient intuition, but to recognize that expertise does not make one person’s knowledge inherently complete and the other's inherently unreliable.

This is the part of medical gaslighting we have been less willing to examine. We talk about what happens when patients are not believed. We should also ask what happens to the person who becomes accustomed to being believed. If we want to understand why some patients keep falling through the cracks, we may need to look at what has been happening on the other side of the desk.

item.title: Midlife, but Make It Millenial
item.description:
Midlife

Midlife, but Make It Millenial

Forget sports cars and cheating; have you tried carshares and polyamory?

Posted September 23, 2026

Key points
  • According to Jung, 40 is when we start to process our upbringings and individiate.
  • Millennials were fed old midlife tropes through pop culture
  • Millenials have unique life experiences that require a new kind of crisis.
A classic symbol of the midlife crisis-- a red sports car
Source: Toby Parsons / Pixabay

It's official: Millennials are entering our midlife crisis era. But in true millennial fashion, we’re doing it our own way. We're not buying sports cars or cheating; we’re joining car shares and exploring polyamory.

Compared to previous generations, millennials have less time and resources, and more anxiety and malaise. We grew up on and alongside the internet (boy has that guy changed!). We’re a generation shaped by economic uncertainty and environmental catastrophe. We’re eager to redefine work and family. The changes to these defining life elements mean the old midlife crisis model just doesn’t work for us.

As a teen, in the nineties and early aughts, pop culture taught me the well-worn tropes, like Monica as “Richard’s little speedster” in Friends, and Red’s motorcycle in That 70’s Show. The midlife crisis was rendered more nuanced and profound but still sterotypically in films like American Beauty and Lost in Translation, where Lester Burnham and Bob Harris grapple with mundanity and meaning at life's halfway point.

When I turned 40 this year, I was nothing but excited. I had recently landed a book deal and was nearly recovered from a bout of burnout. I made a birthday bingo card and posted it online so friends could sign up to celebrate by taking me out dancing, or to clean up a beach, or to lose against me in a rigorous game of Scrabble. Perhaps my predicament just had to gestate like a baby, because 40 weeks after my fortieth birthday, my midlife crisis hit me like a tombstone.

It was confounding, because my life is…pretty good. I make decent money and haven't had any serious illnesses or injuries. I live in a safe area, in a country with a robust social safety net. What more could I want? (I mean, other than an end to extreme wealth and poverty, late-stage capitalism, and the military-industrial complex.)

Yet the urge to blow up my little life persists. I fantasize about quitting my comfortable government job, selling my modest bungalow, and starting over somewhere new. And I’m not the only one.

According to Giuntella et al. (2022) data, suicide, sleeping problems, alcohol dependence, concentration difficulties, memory problems, intense job strain, disabling headaches, suicidal feelings, and extreme depression make quadratic hill-shaped patterns peaking at midlife for citizens of rich nations. Clearly, while the old model of the midlife crisis is outdated, we still need some sort of come-to-Jesus moment.

Carl Jung believed that life truly began at 40. He said we spend the first 40 years of our lives learning and attempting to fulfill societal expectations and seeking external validation. Forty is when we begin to process our unique upbringings and circumstances and come to new understandings about ourselves. It’s our second act, when we’re done trying to please others, and become our full authentic selves—if we're lucky. We finally try to figure out what will fulfill us—before it’s too late.

Midlife Millenial, Lindsey Harrington
